issues.legal_issue: Ceiling proceedings may be conducted against an ostensible holder acting for the real holders, and a public company holding the land may itself be treated as a holder.
material_facts: The government grant placed the land with a company in which the former ruler held shares.
The Farm took possession through the company to develop the land and acted as its agent and ostensible holder.
The Farm responded to the ceiling proceedings, while the company and the former ruler participated through it and did not object or appeal.
The company was a public company holding the land under a government lease.
issues.conclusion: The proceedings against the Farm were valid and binding on the company and the former ruler as the real holders; the company was a holder for ceiling purposes.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5 and Explanations I and II of the Ceiling Act, land held in a person’s own right but ostensibly in another’s name is attributed to the real holder, and continued actual cultivatory possession supports a presumption of such holding. Sections 3(9) and 3(17), read with Section 4(33) of the U.P. General Clauses Act, include a government lessee and a company within the relevant definitions. Section 5(4) concerns apportionment among members of specified associations and does not exclude a public company from being a holder.

rule.if: ceiling_proceeding and company_holds_land and farm_possesses_as_agent and farm_responds_for_real_holders

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to determine the amount of land a holder may retain under a ceiling regime.
predicates.company_holds_land: A company holds the land in its own right, including as a lessee from the government.
predicates.farm_possesses_as_agent: Another entity possesses the land for the company and acts as its agent or ostensible holder.
predicates.farm_responds_for_real_holders: The possessor responds to the proceeding on behalf of the real holders.

issues.definition: When a company holds land and an agent-like possessor responds for it in a ceiling proceeding, the proceeding against that possessor binds the real holders.

issues.legal_issue: Land held under a government grant remains subject to ceiling legislation, and rights claimed through subleases or transfers cannot override the grant’s restrictions.
material_facts: The government placed the land with a grantee on terms restricting its use and prohibiting transfer or alienation without government permission, while allowing specified subletting.
The company and later occupants relied on revenue entries, tenancy legislation and payment of land revenue to claim independent tenancy or ownership rights.
The government grant had not been varied or made transferable with government permission.
issues.conclusion: The land was subject to ceiling legislation, and the claimed tenancy rights and transfers could not defeat the grant’s terms; transfers made without the required permission created no independent rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Government Grants Act, as amended for Uttar Pradesh, gives the grant’s terms overriding effect over inconsistent tenancy-law claims, while its subsection (3) preserves the application of legislation relating to land reform and ceilings. Sections 3(9) and 3(17) of the Ceiling Act include a government lessee among holders. Section 18(1)(c) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act addresses the status of a rent-free grantee. The Court relied on Raghubar Dayal v. State of U.P., which treated a government agricultural grant as a lease subject to ceiling legislation.

predicates.government_grant_holds_agricultural_land: A person holds agricultural land under a grant made by the government.
predicates.grant_restricts_transfer: The grant permits only specified use or subletting and restricts transfers without government permission.
predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to determine the amount of land a holder may retain under a ceiling regime.

issues.definition: Land held under a government grant that restricts transfer remains subject to ceiling determination, and inconsistent claims through occupants do not override the grant.

issues.legal_issue: Post-cutoff transfers are excluded from the ceiling calculation unless the party claiming their benefit proves that they were made in good faith for adequate consideration and were not benami.
material_facts: The relevant transfers were made after the statutory cutoff date, including sales and leases to numerous individuals and firms.
The alleged earlier oral leases were unsupported by proof, and the sales were made after a proposed reduction in the ceiling limit had become public.
Many transferees were connected with persons involved in the company and the firms, and the consideration was not duly accounted for in the company’s balance sheet.
The appellate authority and High Court found that the transfers were made to evade the ceiling law and that finding was not vitiated by irrelevant considerations.
issues.conclusion: The transfers were not shown to be bona fide and were liable to be ignored in determining the holder’s surplus land.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(6), its proviso (b), and Explanation II of the Ceiling Act require post-cutoff transfers to be disregarded unless the party claiming their benefit satisfies the prescribed authority that they were in good faith, for adequate consideration, under an irrevocable instrument, and not benami or for the holder’s benefit; the burden rests on that party. The Court declined to disturb the concurrent factual findings in the appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to determine the amount of land a holder may retain under a ceiling regime.
predicates.transfer_after_cutoff: The holder transferred land after the applicable cutoff date.
predicates.claimant_does_not_prove_good_faith_and_a: The person claiming the benefit of the transfer fails to prove that it was made in good faith for adequate consideration and was not benami.

issues.definition: A post-cutoff transfer is ignored in a ceiling calculation when the claimant fails to establish the required bona fides and adequate consideration.

issues.legal_issue: An earlier ceiling order does not bar later ceiling proceedings when the earlier exclusion rested on an apparent mistake rather than a consciously contested adjudication, particularly where the law permits reopening.
material_facts: An earlier order excluded 250 acres on the mistaken premise that a farm school held the land as a separate legal entity.
The company had claimed the land as its own land used for educational purposes, and the school was neither registered as a society nor a separate legal entity.
The company later transferred portions of the land in its own name, and the land remained held by the company when the amended ceiling regime came into force.
The amended regime removed the educational-institution exemption and introduced provisions allowing earlier ceiling findings to be retried; the State had not appealed the earlier order.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order did not bar the later proceedings from including the land in the company’s holding and determining the applicable surplus; the State’s failure to appeal did not prevent that determination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 38-B of the Ceiling Act bars reliance on earlier findings or decisions to prevent retrial under the Act as amended; Section 38-A permits relevant particulars of land to be considered. The Court explained that the ceiling regime’s social-welfare purpose and the absence of a conscious adjudication on a contested issue limit strict application of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It relied on State of U.P. v. Budh Singh (including the 1997 decision), and referred to Ram Lal v. State of U.P. and Kedar Singh v. Addl. District Judge, Varanasi.

predicates.later_ceiling_proceeding_under_amended_l: A later proceeding determines surplus land under an amended ceiling regime.
predicates.earlier_exclusion_resting_on_apparent_mi: An earlier order excluded land on a factual premise inconsistent with how the holder itself treated the land.
predicates.no_conscious_contested_adjudication: The earlier exclusion did not result from a conscious adjudication of an issue contested between the parties.

issues.definition: A mistaken earlier exclusion that was not consciously contested does not prevent a later proceeding under amended law from reconsidering the land’s inclusion.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee entitled to a hearing in ceiling proceedings need not receive a remand when the transferee later receives a full opportunity to be heard and no different outcome is realistically available.
material_facts: The transferees whose purchases could be adversely affected were not joined or heard in the appellate ceiling proceedings.
The transferees later brought writ petitions and received a detailed opportunity to present evidence and arguments about good faith and consideration.
The High Court examined their evidence and found that the transfers were intended to evade the ceiling law.

The transfers also violated the government grant’s restriction on transfer without permission, and the affected parties had an opportunity to address that legal issue before the High Court and Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The transferees were entitled to be parties and heard in the appellate proceedings, so the procedure was defective; however, the defect did not require setting aside the proceedings or remanding the cases because they later received a full hearing and no different merits outcome was likely.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(6), Explanation II of the Ceiling Act places the burden on a party claiming the benefit of a transfer, making an affected transferee a necessary party entitled to an opportunity to be heard. Natural justice serves substantial justice, and a remand is unnecessary where a full later hearing has addressed the relevant issues and would not change the result. The Court referred to State of Andhra Pradesh v. S. Vishwanatha Raju and considered its discretionary powers under Article 136 of the Constitution.

rule.if: ceiling_appeal and transferee_adversely_affected and transferee_not_heard_initially and full_later_hearing and no_realistic_different_outcome

predicates.ceiling_appeal: An appeal is brought in a proceeding determining surplus land under a ceiling regime.
predicates.transferee_adversely_affected: The decision may invalidate or otherwise adversely affect a transferee’s claimed rights in land.
predicates.transferee_not_heard_initially: The transferee is not joined or given an opportunity to be heard in the initial appeal.
predicates.full_later_hearing: The transferee later receives a full opportunity to present evidence and arguments on the affected issues.
predicates.no_realistic_different_outcome: The later hearing establishes that a remand would not realistically produce a different result on the merits.

issues.definition: A failure to hear an affected transferee initially does not require remand if the transferee later receives a full hearing and the merits leave no realistic prospect of a different result.

issues.legal_issue: Damages for use and occupation of surplus land must be determined through the prescribed statutory process and cannot be imposed as lump-sum costs.
material_facts: The High Court imposed a lump-sum amount as costs, treating it in substance as damages for the Farm’s prolonged use and occupation of surplus land.
The ceiling law provided for compensation for use and occupation and the rules prescribed principles for quantifying it through separate proceedings.
The High Court also made an individual managing partner liable if the Farm defaulted, although he acted in his capacity as a partner.
issues.conclusion: The lump-sum costs imposed as damages, including the direction making the managing partner liable on default, were set aside; quantification was a matter for the ceiling authorities under the prescribed process.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Ceiling Act provides for compensation for use and occupation of surplus land, and Rule 18A prescribes principles for its quantification. Those provisions require separate proceedings before the ceiling authorities, rather than an award of lump-sum damages disguised as costs.

predicates.ceiling_case: A case concerns the determination or enforcement of surplus land under a ceiling regime.
predicates.court_imposes_lump_sum_costs_as_occupati: A court imposes costs that function in substance as a lump-sum award for use and occupation of surplus land.
predicates.law_requires_separate_quantification: The governing regime requires the amount of occupation damages to be assessed through a separate prescribed process.

issues.definition: When a court uses costs to impose occupation damages that must be separately assessed, the lump-sum damages order is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee cannot claim better rights than the original transferee whose title or claim has been rejected.
material_facts: Later purchasers and other successors claimed rights through the original transferees whose transfers were found invalid or liable to be ignored.
The subsequent transferees did not establish an independent basis for rights superior to those of their transferors.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent transferees were entitled to no relief based on their derivative claims; any independent rights of other interveners had to be pursued separately.
issues.legal_principle: A successor taking through a transferee acquires no better derivative claim than that transferee. The Court did not adjudicate any independent rights that interveners might pursue through other remedies.

predicates.subsequent_transferee: A person acquires land or asserts rights through an earlier transferee.
predicates.transferor_claim_rejected: The earlier transferee’s claim to the land is rejected or affords no relief.
predicates.no_independent_superior_basis: The successor shows no independent basis for a right superior to the transferor’s claim.

issues.definition: A subsequent transferee whose transferor’s claim is rejected and who shows no independent superior basis has no better derivative right.
